candidate.answerReason: A 31-day month has four full weeks and three extra weekdays. The only three consecutive weekdays containing neither Tuesday nor Saturday are Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday.

methods.label: Count full weeks and extra days
methods.explanation:
January has \(31=4\cdot7+3\) days. Its first \(28\) days form four complete weeks, giving four of every weekday. The remaining three dates, January \(29\), \(30\), and \(31\), have the same weekdays as January \(1\), \(2\), and \(3\). Those three weekdays therefore occur five times.

Since Tuesday and Saturday occur exactly four times, neither can be among the first three weekdays of January. Around the week, the weekdays avoiding Tuesday and Saturday form two uninterrupted groups: Wednesday, Thursday, Friday; and Sunday, Monday. Only the first group contains three consecutive weekdays.

Thus January \(1\) was \(\boxed{\text{Wednesday}}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
methods.levelReason: Uses full weeks, leftover days, and elementary elimination among weekday possibilities.

candidate.annotationRationale: Grouping 31 days into full weeks and leftover days fits applications of division with remainders. The weekday restrictions then force a unique starting day through finite constraint deduction. Calendar month length and the meaning of a remainder support the method; formal congruences are not used.

review.mathematicalCheck: Four complete weeks account for 28 days, so precisely the first three day names occur five times. Avoiding Tuesday and Saturday leaves Wednesday through Friday as the unique consecutive triple, forcing January 1 to be Wednesday.
review.levelCheck: The explanation uses elementary weekly grouping and clearly justifies uniqueness without formal congruences.
review.annotationCheck: Division with remainders and finite constraint deduction match the reasoning. Calendar facts and remainder meaning are suitable shared support; formal modular congruence is appropriately omitted.
